lessons.title: Numeric sort and mutation
lessons.summary: Return a new ascending sorted array of finite numbers, preserving the source. Use a numeric comparator; empty input returns a new empty array.
explanation: sort() without a comparator compares string representations, so numbers can appear in an unexpected order. A numeric comparator (a, b) => a - b returns a negative number when a belongs before b, zero for equal order, and a positive number when a belongs after b. It must be consistent; returning only true/false is not the same contract.

array.sort(comparator) rearranges that array in place and returns the same array reference. array.slice() with no arguments returns a shallow copy. Sorting the copy preserves the caller’s order; nested objects, if present, would still be shared. This exercise accepts finite numbers only, avoiding NaN and mixed-type ordering.

Implement numericCopy without modifying values, including empty input. Optional practice: change a-b to b-a and explain why the sign reversal produces descending order, without predicting a particular sort implementation’s comparison sequence.

lessons.title: Object entries and reconstruction
lessons.summary: Double each own enumerable string-keyed finite numeric property into a new object. Preserve the source; exclude inherited properties. Empty input returns an empty object.
explanation: Object.entries(object) returns an array of [key,value] pairs for own enumerable string-keyed properties. Inherited properties and symbol keys are excluded. Here the input is a plain data object with finite numeric own values; no getters or hostile proxies are part of the contract.

Object.fromEntries(pairs) takes an iterable of key/value pairs and returns a new ordinary object. Repeated keys keep the last supplied value. This builds an object; it does not modify the source or install a sanitization policy. The loop’s [key,value] syntax destructures each pair; pairs.push(pair) appends one pair and returns the array’s new length, which we ignore.
Implement doubleOwn by transforming entries, not by iterating inherited names. Optional practice: call Object.fromEntries([["read",1],["read",5]]) and explain why the resulting own read value is5.

lessons.title: Unicode code units and code points
lessons.summary: Return {units:text.length, points:number_of_for_of_iterations} for a well-formed Unicode string. Preserve text exactly; do not normalize or call code-point count a visible-character count.
explanation: A JavaScript string’s length counts UTF-16 code units. Many characters use one unit, but a supplementary code point such as 🌱 uses a surrogate pair: two units. Neither this length nor code-point count necessarily equals the number of visible grapheme clusters.

for...of over a string yields strings representing Unicode code points rather than splitting a valid surrogate pair. textCounts(text) counts those iterations and returns {units,points}. The shortened property points means points: points. This exercise uses well-formed Unicode strings; it does not repair isolated surrogates or normalize combining marks.

Use the count that answers your actual question. Code-point iteration is not full grapheme segmentation. Optional practice: compare "é" and "e\u0301" and explain why visually similar text can have different counts without changing either input.

lessons.title: Class inheritance and super
lessons.summary: Implement TimedTask extending the supplied Task. Initialize title through super, store minutes, and override describe to return the parent description followed by " / N min". Inputs meet the stated string/number contract.
explanation: extends establishes an inheritance relationship. TimedTask instances can use Task behavior and add their own minutes. A derived constructor must call super(...) before accessing this; that call initializes the instance through the parent constructor.

TimedTask.describe overrides the inherited method. super.describe() calls the parent implementation with the same instance as its receiver. It returns the title text; the override adds duration text. Calling this.describe() from this override instead would recurse into itself, not select the parent method.
Keep Task unchanged and implement TimedTask. Optional practice: assign a different title after construction and predict why the parent method reads the current title from the same instance.

lessons.title: Getters and setters
lessons.summary: Implement Session with a minutes getter/setter. Accept only integers 0..60; throw RangeError before changing state otherwise. Constructor initialization must use the same validation. Backing field _minutes is conventional, not private.
explanation: A getter runs when a property is read; a setter runs when it is assigned. session.minutes uses property syntax, not session.minutes(). get minutes() returns a value; set minutes(value) receives the assigned value. A setter’s return value is not how the assigned value is read.

The setter uses Number.isInteger(value), which returns a Boolean without converting strings, then enforces the inclusive 0..60 range. new RangeError(message) constructs an error and throw transfers control to the caller. Only after validation do we store _minutes, so a rejected assignment preserves the old state. The underscore is just a naming convention, not access control.
Implement the class with one validation path used for initialization and later assignment. Optional practice: try the string "5" and explain why it is rejected rather than silently converted.

lessons.title: Private fields and static members
lessons.summary: Implement Counter with private #value, constructor(initial), add(amount), read(), and static zero(). Each zero() call returns a distinct instance at0. Inputs are finite numbers; add mutates only its receiver and returns its new value.
explanation: #value is a private field declared in the class body. Methods of this class access it as this.#value. It is not the same as a public property named "#value", and outside code cannot directly write first.#value. This is language-level encapsulation, not encryption or a promise that an object can safely hold secrets against all program code.

static zero() is called on Counter, not on an instance. It takes no arguments and returns a fresh Counter initialized to0. Each constructor call creates separate private state. add(amount) adds the supplied finite number and returns the updated value; read() returns the current value with no mutation.

Implement Counter with the declared private field and the class-bound zero factory. Optional practice: compare Counter.zero().read() with new Counter(7).read(). An external private-field access is rejected by the parser; do not paste invalid syntax into the main runnable solution.

lessons.title: Property descriptors and shallow freeze
lessons.summary: Return a frozen outer object with own version=1 (enumerable, non-writable, non-configurable) and theme={dark:false}. The nested theme remains mutable. No deep-freeze claim.
explanation: Object.defineProperty(object,name,descriptor) defines an own property and returns that same object. A data descriptor supplies value plus writable, enumerable and configurable flags. Here version is visible to ordinary own-key enumeration, but cannot be assigned a new value or deleted/reconfigured. Omitted flags default to false for a newly defined property.

Object.freeze(object) returns that same object after preventing new own properties and making its own data properties non-writable and non-configurable. It does not recursively freeze a nested object. In this lesson theme still refers to a mutable inner object. A const binding alone would not apply these property restrictions.

Implement the outer frozen settings object while keeping the nested theme object unfrozen. Optional practice: explain why replacing settings.theme and editing settings.theme.dark are different operations.

lessons.title: Finally and custom error causes
lessons.summary: Implement readLabel with the supplied LoadError class. Return a valid string label; wrap JSON parse or wrong-label-type failures with new LoadError("Cannot load label", originalCause). Append "finished" exactly once on success or failure.
explanation: A custom LoadError extends Error. super(message,{cause}) supplies the error message and retains the original thrown value in the cause property; {cause} is shorthand for {cause:cause}. Setting name makes the diagnostic category explicit. Constructing an error does not throw it until throw is used.

readLabel(raw,events) parses JSON text, returns a string label if valid, or throws a LoadError wrapping a parse/shape failure. JSON.parse returns a decoded value or throws SyntaxError. The explicit type guard rejects non-string labels with TypeError. finally appends "finished" to the supplied event array whether the try returned or threw; push returns the new length, which we ignore.

A return or throw inside finally can replace an earlier result or failure, so this finally only records completion. Optional practice: use valid {"label":"Sky"} input and explain why the returned string and the finished event both occur.

lessons.title: DOM attributes and class tokens
lessons.summary: Using the supplied button element, set aria-pressed to the text form of active and force only its active class token on/off. Return whether that token is present afterward. Preserve existing class tokens and text; active is a Boolean.
explanation:
This lesson requires a DOM document containing the following button. DOM APIs belong to the document host, not plain Node JavaScript. A DOM harness can verify attributes/classes but does not prove browser layout, assistive-technology announcements or real keyboard interaction.
```html
<button id="toggle" class="control" aria-pressed="false">Focus</button>
```

setAttribute(name,value) writes the named attribute and returns undefined. getAttribute(name) reads its string value or null if absent. String(active) converts the supplied Boolean to "true" or "false" for aria-pressed. ARIA state describes this button’s toggle state; it does not automatically install an event handler.

button.classList is a token-list view of its class attribute. toggle("active",active) uses the Boolean second argument to add or remove that one token and returns whether it is present afterward. Calling it twice with true leaves the token present; it is not an inversion each time. contains(token) returns membership without changing the list. Other tokens, such as control, remain untouched.

Implement setActive without replacing the entire class attribute or changing button text. Optional practice: call it twice with true, then once with false, and explain why unrelated classes remain. Check for null when selecting from an uncertain page outside this fixed fixture.
